post.summary: Queue an on-demand creative analysis
post.description:
Ask for one ad's creative to be analysed now, instead of waiting for the daily background pass. **This never runs a model on the request; it queues one.** The response is a receipt, and the analysis itself arrives through `GET` on this same path — which is what `Location` points at.

**Two ceilings gate ADMISSION**, both per UTC day and both configurable per tenant: 20 analyses per profile and 100 per API key by default. Exceeding either answers `429` with `Retry-After` set to the seconds remaining until the next UTC midnight; the message names which ceiling fired, the counters, and the reset instant. This is separate from — and additional to — the ordinary per-minute rate limit, and the endpoint also carries its own hourly burst cap.

**A third limit gates the RUN, and it is a different resource: the workspace's daily creative-analysis allowance**, shared with the background pass and set by the plan. An admitted job whose workspace has already spent today's allowance is NOT refused and NOT failed — it stays `queued` and waits for the allowance to refill at the next 00:00 UTC, then runs. It waits at most one day: if the allowance is still spent after that reset the job ends `blocked`, which costs nothing against the two admission ceilings above and can be re-requested. So a `202` promises the analysis will be attempted, not that it will be attempted today.

**Idempotent for 24 hours.** The key is the ad plus its creative: the ad's name, headline, body, video and thumbnail. A second POST inside that window, with none of those changed, returns the SAME job with `200` and `reused: true` and consumes no budget. A new job is admitted with `202`. Edit the creative and the next POST is a new job, which is the behaviour you want — the old analysis describes an ad that no longer exists.

**No request body.** The ad is in the path and the caller is in the credential; there is nothing else to say, and in particular there is no way to ask for a re-run of an unchanged creative or to exceed the budget.

The scope is `creatives:write`, which no OAuth connect scope grants by default — a workspace admin opts a key into it. A read credential cannot cause AI spend.

schema.description: The ad's platform/external id.

parameters.description: The ad's platform/external id.
parameters.name: id

200.description: An existing job for this ad and this creative was returned instead (`reused: true`). Nothing new was queued and no budget was consumed.

202.description: A new job was admitted and is queued. `Location` is the GET on this path — poll it for the analysis.

404.description: No ad with that external id belongs to this key's profile.

429.description: A daily budget is exhausted (per profile or per API key), or the endpoint's own hourly burst cap was hit. `Retry-After` carries the wait in seconds.

post.summary: Mark a profile's back catalogue for creative analysis
post.description:
"Analyze history" — ask the daily background creative-analysis pass to work through ads that predate it. **This marks ads; it never runs a model.** `rpc_request_creative_analysis_backfill` stamps every ad with spend in the chosen lookback window that has no current-version analysis, and the every-2-hours cron drains the marked ads inside the workspace's daily `creative_analysis` allowance (shared with the ordinary background pass). So the honest answer to "how much can I backfill?" is a number of days, which is what `estimated_days` is.

**`dry_run` defaults to `true`.** A dry run previews the plan without marking anything; `dry_run: false` commits it — `marked` ads get `creative_analysis_requested_at` stamped and `applied` flips to `true`.

Nothing is written to `outcome_events` yet — the parsed rows are stashed on a draft `payment_imports` row (`status: "preview"`) that `POST .../import/commit` reads back by `import_id`.

post.summary: Commit a previously-parsed payments import
post.description:
Write the rows a prior `POST .../import/parse` staged (named by `import_id`) into `outcome_events` as `payment_received`. For `transbank_webpay`, deduplicated on `(profile_id, external_source, external_id)` where `external_id` is derived from Transbank's own `buy_order` + `authorization_code` — the same key the live Webpay passthrough uses, so a payment already ingested live is skipped rather than double-counted. For `offline_sales`, deduplicated on the mapped deal/order id when the sheet has one, else a hash of (sale date, amount, currency, customer identity) — see `@atribu/analytics-enrichment/payments/offline-sales-processor`'s header for the full reasoning on both failure directions this key balances. Refuses with `409` when `conversion_goal_ok` (echoed at parse time) is false — writing rows that would never become a counted conversion is worse than refusing (data-model.md #437). Each inserted row resolves (or creates) the customer's profile from the row's name/email/phone. On success with at least one insert, an interactive attribution recompute is enqueued.

`mapping` may only be supplied unchanged from what `.../import/parse` returned — changing it at commit time answers `409` asking for a re-upload (v1 limitation: the raw file rows are not retained past parse). `save_mapping` persists the column mapping for future imports on this profile (per provider).

post.summary: Analyse one ad entity's performance
post.description:
A live, model-written analysis of how one campaign, ad set or ad is PERFORMING — its strengths, weaknesses and concrete suggestions, grounded in that entity's own spend, delivery and Atribu-attributed cash outcomes over the window you name. `{id}` is the entity's EXTERNAL (platform) id and `level` says which table it lives in.

**This SPENDS the workspace's AI allowance and nothing is stored.** Each call runs a model and writes an `ai_usage_log` row; with `include_video: true` it runs a frontier multimodal model over the ad's video, which is the most expensive single operation on this API. Requesting the same analysis twice costs twice. It is bounded by the workspace's daily allowance, by a per-credential hourly cap, and by per-principal and per-profile burst limits.

**Not to be confused with `GET /api/v1/ads/{id}/creative-analysis`**, which serves the STORED creative fingerprint a scheduled background pass produced (what the creative SAYS). This one is about what the numbers DID, and it is computed on the request.

Video analysis degrades rather than fails: `video_status` says whether it was requested, whether it happened, and if not, why — the copy analysis is returned either way.

post.summary: Run the UTM health audit now
post.description:
Runs the live UTM/tracking-health scan for the profile and returns the summary it just computed. This is the write counterpart to `GET /api/v1/quality/utm`, which only ever reads whatever the daily cron last cached.

SYNCHRONOUS. The scan takes roughly 8-12 seconds on a large profile and the response is terminal — there is no job id and nothing to poll. Hold the connection open.

IDEMPOTENT WITHIN 10 MINUTES. If the cached summary's `refreshed_at` is younger than 10 minutes the scan is skipped and the cached row is returned with `refreshed: false`. Send `{"force": true}` to scan anyway; the rate limit still applies.

RATE LIMIT. Beyond the per-key per-minute allowance (this route is a `heavy` 3-unit call) it carries its own bucket of 6 scans per hour per key, because one call is 8-12 seconds of database work. A 429 from that bucket carries `Retry-After`.

`days` selects the scan window and is capped to the Ephemeral Buffer's retention (30 days, ADR 0014 d2) — the row this writes is keyed on it, so a wider request is rejected (400) rather than silently narrowed.

parameters.description: Scan window. 1-30, default 30.
parameters.name: days

400.description: Invalid body, or ?days= exceeds the Ephemeral Buffer window

429.description: Rate limited — either the per-minute key allowance or this route's own 6-per-hour scan bucket. Both send `Retry-After`.

504.description: `audit_timeout` — the scan did not finish inside the request budget. Retry after the `Retry-After` interval; the last cached summary remains readable from `GET /api/v1/quality/utm`.

The per-issue detail behind `GET /api/v1/quality/utm`'s `high_count` / `medium_count`: what each issue is, how much traffic it affects, the top offending values observed, and the suggested fix.

A CACHED read, like the badge — it never runs the scan. The scan is `POST /api/v1/quality/utm/refresh`, which is `attribution:write` precisely because it writes. Call the refresh first if you need a live answer, then read this; the refresh response deliberately returns only the summary, so the breakdown is always this second call.

FRESHNESS IS ITS OWN. `refreshed_at` here dates the anomaly list, and it can be older than the badge's `refreshed_at` on the same profile: the daily cron recounts the badge cheaply and does not recompute the breakdown. `null` means the deep scan has never run for this window, which is not the same as a clean profile.

`?days=` selects which cached window to read and is capped to the Ephemeral Buffer's retention (30 days, ADR 0014 d2) — the row this backs can never exist for a wider window, so a wider request is rejected (400) rather than silently answered with nothing.

The deliveries ledger — one row per (conversion × destination × rule) the export pipeline has considered, newest first. The same data the Conversion Sync Deliveries view shows, minus everything that identifies a person.

**Excluded by construction**: the platform payload (which carries hashed email/phone/name plus an unhashed IP address and user agent), the Click-to-WhatsApp click id, the customer's name/email/phone, and the provider's raw error message. What remains is delivery identity and outcome: the ledger row, its canonical event id, the status ladder, the attempt count, the provider's trace id and latency, and an error CLASS.

`date_from` / `date_to` window the DELIVERY ATTEMPT (`created_at`), not the source conversion's event time — the opposite of `POST /api/v1/exports`, which windows the conversion. Both are inclusive of whole UTC days.

Pagination is keyset: pass the returned `pagination.cursor` back as `?cursor=`. `status_counts` is a rollup over the WINDOW and deliberately ignores `?status=`, so a filtered request can still show its own share of the whole.

post.summary: Trigger a conversion export
post.description:
Schedule an export run for a set of conversions, either by date range (`date_from` + `date_to`, windowing the SOURCE conversion's event time) or by explicit `conversion_ids`. Exactly one of the two forms — a body carrying both is rejected rather than silently interpreted.

**This queues work; it does not send.** The export pipeline performs the actual upload, which is what keeps deduplication, the privacy/HIPAA guard, the platform staleness window and the retry ceiling in one implementation. Returns `202` with a batch id; poll `GET /api/v1/exports/{id}` for what happened.

**Idempotent, and the response says how.** A conversion already delivered under its canonical event id — including one that shipped via a different ingestion path for the same real booking — is reported as `already_delivered` and is never re-sent. One that a queued job is already going to pick up is `already_queued`. So repeating the same request is a no-op: the second call reports the same conversions as already queued and schedules nothing.

`counts.enqueued` is a count of deliveries SCHEDULED, never of events the platform received.

Blocked with `409 invalid_state` when the profile's legal gate is unsatisfied (HIPAA without a signed BAA, Platform-Safe without an accepted DPA).

**`require_approval: true` puts a person between you and the send.** You still get `202`, but nothing is queued: `data` is `{status: "awaiting_approval", handoff}`. Give `handoff.url` to your user — the page is session-less, works on a phone and expires in 45 minutes — and poll `GET /api/v1/handoffs/{id}` until `status` leaves `pending`. That is how an agency's agent routes every Meta write on a client account past the client.

202.description: The export run was scheduled — or, with `require_approval: true`, a hand-off is waiting for a human and nothing was queued.

400.description: Invalid body, or both request forms supplied

409.description: The profile's legal gate blocks exporting

post.description:
Map one conversion definition to one platform event. Preview it first with `POST /api/v1/exports/rules/preview`.

**`value_mode: "none"` on a value-required Meta event is rejected** (422). Meta documents `value` + `currency` as required for `Purchase`, so such a rule can only ever emit a payload Meta refuses — one profile shipped that config for a month and lost 152 Purchases to dead letters, 306 of them permanently, because Meta's replay window is 7 days.

post.summary: Create several conversion-export signal rules
post.description:
Create up to 50 rules in one call — what a review screen confirms after choosing several outcomes at once. Each row is the body `POST /api/v1/exports/rules` takes and is validated exactly as that route validates it.

**All-or-report, not all-or-nothing.** Every row is created or refused on its own and the answer carries one result per row, in request order: `created` with the rule, or `rejected` with the code and message the single create would have answered. One bad row never blocks the others, and no row is dropped. The status is 200 whatever the mix; only a malformed envelope is 422.

One export pass is queued for the whole batch, and only when at least one rule was created. Send an `Idempotency-Key` to make a retried confirm replay the first report instead of creating every rule again.

A dry run over the last 7 days: how many source records a candidate rule would have matched, and which Meta event it would emit. Writes nothing and needs only `exports:read`.

`candidate_count` is an UPPER BOUND on the rule's effect, never a forecast of deliveries — a matched record still has to clear identity, the privacy guard, the platform's staleness window and destination routing.

Partial update. `source_kind` is immutable. Set `archived_at` to retire a rule that has export history and therefore cannot be deleted.

The value-mode check runs against the MERGED rule, not the patch: a body that only sets `value_mode: "none"` on a Purchase rule is exactly the change that guard exists to refuse.

A `stage_exited` rule fires on leaving `from_stage` (required); an optional `to_stage` narrows it to leaving towards that stage. `fixed_value` + `fixed_currency` on a `fixed_value` rule.

Absent, that lane uses Atribu's default map by source event type (e.g. lead_created → LeadSubmitted, appointment_booked → QualifiedLead, payment_received → Purchase) and skips a type with no messaging equivalent.

post.summary: Send a Meta test event
post.description:
Post ONE synthetic event to the configured Meta dataset with a `test_event_code`, so it lands in Events Manager → Test Events and nowhere else. The last step of setup: destination → rule → test → export.

It carries the `atribu_src` marker a production event carries, so it actually exercises the Custom Conversion a rule created — a test that skipped it would fire the pixel and not the conversion, which is the most misleading possible result while verifying a setup.

Returns Meta's response verbatim. `quality_warning` is non-null when this profile's match-quality policy would block a real event carrying only what a test carries (IP + user agent); the test still sends.

`test_event_code` is required: a send without one would be a real conversion on the live dataset, so it is refused with `422 validation_error` before Meta is called.

Capped at 5 sends per profile per minute. Blocked with `409 invalid_state` when the profile's privacy rules or legal gate refuse the payload — nothing reached Meta, and `error.reason` names the gate's reason (e.g. `dpa_not_accepted` for a Platform-Safe profile whose DPA is not accepted, `baa_not_approved` for HIPAA). A `502 provider_error` with `error.reason: meta_rejected` means the event DID reach Meta and Meta refused it.

get.summary: List the accounts a pending connect can be finalized against
get.description:
After a connect flow bounces back with `status=pending_selection`, this returns the accounts / properties / locations the dealer must choose between, so you can render the picker in your own UI.

**You only reach this when a choice is genuinely required.** When the consent resolves to exactly one candidate the callback finalizes it itself and returns `status=success`, which means CONNECTED — read the connection back, do not call this.

The provider token behind the pending selection lives for 60 minutes (`expires_at`). Past that, and for a profile with nothing pending for this provider, the answer is 404 with the same message: there is no pending selection here, start the connect flow again.

Scope: `attribution:write` — the same scope the `attribution_write` connect grant mints. This is a step of a connect, not an analytics read, and the candidate list is the only thing the parked token authorizes.

schema.description: The `connection_provider` value — the same string `GET /api/v1/connections` returns as `channel` and the same one stored on the connection. Only these four have a consent-then-pick flow; Google Calendar finalizes inside its own callback.

404.description: No pending connection for this provider on this key's profile — never started, already finalized, or the 60-minute window elapsed. The three are deliberately indistinguishable.

post.summary: Finalize a pending connect with the chosen account
post.description:
Completes the connect: writes the connection, runs every side effect the in-app picker runs (the reporting-currency write for Meta, the per-location token exchange and conversion-definition seed for GoHighLevel), and discards the parked provider token.

`candidate_id` is a candidate's `id` from `GET /api/v1/connections/pending/{provider}`, verbatim. An id the granted token cannot actually reach is 400 `invalid_parameter`.

**Retries are safe.** The parked token is consumed on success, so a repeat of the SAME `candidate_id` answers 200 with `already_finalized: true` and the existing connection. A DIFFERENT `candidate_id` after the choice has been made is 409 `invalid_state`: switching accounts is a new connect, not a retry, and there is no longer a provider token to write.

Scope: `attribution:write`.

409.description: `invalid_state`: this provider is already connected to a DIFFERENT account. Start a new connect flow to change it. `account_connected_elsewhere` (#1800): the chosen account is already connected to another profile of this workspace; nothing is written and the parked token stays, so a different account can be chosen.

get.summary: List authorized data connections
get.description:
Every connection on this key's profile that it is entitled to see, in two classes told apart by `kind`.

`kind: "messaging"` — WhatsApp, Instagram, email and Google/Microsoft Calendar. For OAuth-flow-minted keys these are restricted to the connections your app holds an active authorization for; for direct admin keys, every one on the profile.

Every other kind — `ad_platform` (Meta Ads, Google Ads, Search Console), `crm` (GoHighLevel), `commerce` (Shopify), `payments` (Stripe, MercadoPago), `integration` (Notion, ManyChat) — is returned for the key's profile regardless of which connection your app was authorized for, because these are connected under a PROFILE-level grant rather than a per-connection one. This is how you confirm that a `POST /api/v1/connections/pending/{provider}/finalize` — or a connect bounce that came back `status=success` — actually produced a connection.

Messaging connections are listed first, then the rest. Neither leg is otherwise ordered.

Every entry carries `sync` — when the connector last completed a run, what it is doing now, and the error text if it failed. That is the whole of a connection-health poll, so there is no separate health endpoint; narrow it with `?channel=` when you only care about one. Rows in every status are returned, `disconnected` included.

get.description:
Returns one connection by id, in the same shape the list returns it — every `kind`, not only `messaging`.

delete.summary: Revoke this OAuth app's authorization for a connection
delete.description:
Marks your app's `oauth_app_authorizations` row for this connection as revoked, **and revokes every API key that authorization minted** — both the keys issued by the authorization-code exchange and the ones issued by `client_credentials` against it. `revoked_keys` says how many.

**When this is your app's LAST live authorization on the profile**, older key generations that no authorization names are revoked with it. Those are keys minted before authorizations recorded which keys they issued; while your app holds another authorization here they are left alone, so revoking one connection of several never touches them.

**This usually includes the key you are calling with.** The request itself completes — the key was validated before the revoke ran — but the next request with it answers 401, within seconds. A key minted under a DIFFERENT authorization of the same app (another connection on the same profile) is untouched and keeps working. To keep acting for the profile after revoking one connection, hold a separate key per authorization or mint a fresh one through `client_credentials`.

Does NOT disconnect the underlying data connection — other OAuth apps and the workspace UI continue to use it. Only messaging connections can be revoked here: any other `kind` answers 404, exactly as an unknown id does. Direct admin keys have no authorization row and reject this call with 400.

Idempotent: revoking an already-revoked authorization, or one now held by a newer key generation than yours, answers 200 with `revoked_keys: 0`.

200.description: Authorization revoked, with the number of API keys it cut

400.description: Direct admin keys cannot self-revoke

404.description: Authorization or connection not found

422.description: `id` is not a UUID.

get.summary: List the Meta pixels on an ad-account connection
get.description:
The pixels (datasets) on a `meta_ads` connection's ad account, so you can pick the `meta_pixel_id` that `POST /api/v1/exports/destinations` requires.

**Why this exists.** A delegated key had no way to discover a pixel id: `GET /api/v1/conversion-sync/dataset` only reconciles a dataset that is *already* configured, and `POST /api/v1/conversion-sync/setup-links` mints a console link for a signed-in human and refuses API keys. Without this read the only way to finish a Conversion Sync setup over the API was to ask the account owner to copy an id out of Events Manager.

One live Meta Graph call per request, and **never cached** — you are about to write a destination against the answer, so a pixel deleted or disabled since must not still be on offer.

`id` is the only field Meta always returns; everything else is `null` when Meta did not answer it. `null` is not `false` — see `is_unavailable`.

404 for an id on another profile and for an id that does not exist; the two are deliberately indistinguishable. A connection that exists but is not `meta_ads` answers 409 rather than 404, because you can read that same row through `GET /api/v1/connections/{id}` and pretending it is missing would be a lie.

200.description: The ad account's pixels. An account with none answers `200` with an empty list.

401.description: The connection has no usable Meta token, or Meta rejected it (code 190). Carries `reconnect_required` and the hand-off action to call.

404.description: Connection not found or not on this key's profile

409.description: `invalid_state` — the connection exists but is not a `meta_ads` connection.

422.description: `id` is not a UUID.

502.description: Meta answered with an error this API could not classify.

get.summary: Get attribution trust signals
get.description:
The three measurements behind the dashboard's Trust panel, in one document: how much of the profile's cash is traceable to an ad (`cash_coverage`), whether the instrumentation producing that number is sound (`instrumentation`), and which way the traceable half is moving (`traceable_roas_trend`).

THEY ARE ONE ANSWER, WHICH IS WHY THEY ARE ONE ROUTE. `cash_coverage` alone reads as an indictment — "only 34% of your cash is traceable" — when the honest reading may be "you have great organic". `instrumentation.tracking_healthy` is what tells the two apart, and `coverage_interpretation` states the verdict in one field.

THREE DIFFERENT WINDOWS, on purpose. `cash_coverage` uses `date_from`/`date_to` (echoed in `meta`). `instrumentation` uses `?days=` (default 30) and is capped to the Ephemeral Buffer's retention (30 days, ADR 0014 d2) because one of its signals reads that buffer — a wider request is rejected (400) rather than silently narrowed. `traceable_roas_trend` uses `?window_days=` (default 28), always ENDING TODAY and split in half: a directional read whose comparison must not jitter with a caller-chosen range.

NO VERDICT IS DERIVED HERE. Scale/hold/cut guidance is a judgement over these facts and stays out of the API.

get.summary: List a customer's payments with their first-payment flags
get.description:
Every `payment_received` conversion for one customer, newest first, each with the effective `is_first_payment` flag and the stored `manual_override` beside it.

**No date range.** This is the customer's whole payment history, which is the only window in which "is this their first payment?" has an answer — windowing it would let a payment look like a first because the real first one fell outside the range.

A customer id this key's profile does not own is 404, indistinguishable from one that does not exist. A customer who exists here but has no payments yet is 200 with `[]`.

Scope: `customers:read`. This is the PII tier and there is no masked variant — the response IS one named person's payment history, so a key without the scope is refused rather than served a redacted copy.

post.summary: Set or clear a payment's first-payment override
post.description:
Pins one payment as (or as not) the customer's first, overriding the derived flag; `manual_override: null` CLEARS the override and hands the payment back to the derivation.

The write recomputes `is_first_payment` for **every** payment of this customer, not just the named one — clearing an override can hand first-payment status back to a different row — so re-read `GET /api/v1/customers/{id}/payments` for the new picture rather than assuming only the posted payment moved.

**Idempotent.** Posting the override a payment already carries writes nothing and answers 200 with `changed: false`; a real change answers `changed: true`. Saying the same thing twice is not an error, and a retry after a dropped response must not read as one.

`outcome_event_id` must name a payment of the customer in the path — a payment belonging to someone else is 404, the same answer an unknown customer gets.

Scope: `attribution:write`. This moves LTV cohorts, the first-payment-vs-recurring revenue split and the CAC denominator; a read scope must never reach it.

get.summary: Get attribution coverage — how many conversions can be attributed at all
get.description:
Splits the window's non-reversal conversions into three buckets by how much tracking they carry: a real ad identifier, an `fbclid` only, or nothing. The three PARTITION `total_conversions` — every conversion lands in exactly one — so they sum to it.

This is the CONVERSION-side companion to `GET /api/v1/quality/utm`, which scores TRAFFIC (anomalous or missing UTMs on visits, plus ad ids that resolve to no known ad). A profile can score well on one and badly on the other, which is when reading both matters; they are kept as separate routes rather than merged so neither average hides the other.

Unlike `/quality/utm` this read is NOT bounded by the Ephemeral Buffer's 30-day retention: it scans `conversions`, a durable table. Any range up to 366 days is valid.

`filter[<dimension>]=<operator>:<value>` (#628) narrows it to the same slice `/api/v1/breakdown` would report, so the coverage number reconciles with a filtered dashboard.

get.summary: Get when this profile's attribution data was last recomputed
get.description:
The freshness behind a "data updated" badge, and the number to poll between recomputes.

It is the ATTRIBUTION PROJECTION's watermark, **not** an ad platform connector's last sync. The two routinely differ by hours and users read "last updated" as *their data's* freshness, so only this one is published under that name.

No date range: this is a property of the profile, not of a window.

get.summary: List the profile's outcome and conversion definitions
get.description:
The two catalogs a goal selector is built from, in one response — because which one to use is the thing consumers get wrong.

`conversion_definitions` are the actual CONVERSION TYPES, with `revenue_type` and `attribution_eligible`. Build a goal selector from these, and match them against the `goal` filter dimension (`conversion_key` === `conversions.conversion_type`).

`outcome_definitions` are CRM pipeline-stage LABELS — user-facing names such as "Descualificado". They name the buckets outcome COUNTS are keyed by; they carry no revenue or attribution semantics and are not goals. They are deduplicated by `event_key` (one key can have a row per CRM pipeline).

This is a READ at `analytics:read`. The write-scoped CRUD collection over `conversion_definitions` is `/api/v1/goals` and is a separate surface.

No date range: a catalogue is not windowed.

post.summary: Create one conversion definition
post.description:
Defines what counts as a conversion: which raw `outcome_events.event_type` values produce it, whether its value is cash, and whether it may receive attribution credit.

**Source event names are unique across the profile's definitions.** An overlap answers 409 and names the definition that already claims the event — two definitions over one event would double-count it in every report.

Stamps an audit row and queues one full-profile replay: a definition change re-derives the profile's conversions from its stored outcome events, so past periods change too.

Preview with `POST /api/v1/goals/definitions/preview` first — `revenue_sum` there is the raw event-value total, not revenue.

409.description: A source event name is already claimed by another definition

422.description: Malformed body, an empty condition set, or an output_channel not in the taxonomy

get.summary: Count the profile's outcome events in a window, by type
get.description:
How many of each outcome type happened between two dates — the numbers a goal selector ranks and labels its options with.

**Read it together with `GET /api/v1/goals/definitions`, which is a CATALOGUE and carries no numbers.** The catalogue says what a goal IS (`revenue_type`, `attribution_eligible`, the `conversion_key` a `goal` filter matches on); this says which goals actually occurred in the range the user is looking at. A picker built from one alone is wrong in a different way each time: from the catalogue only it offers goals with nothing behind them, from the counts only it has no labels and no revenue semantics.

**The keys are `event_type`s, not conversion keys.** They usually coincide — a `conversion_definitions` row normally lists its own name in `source_event_names` — but they are separate vocabularies, and `conversion_definitions` remains the goal catalogue.

**Counts, not conversions.** These are raw `outcome_events` rows: they are not deduplicated against `conversions`, carry no revenue, and are not attribution-filtered. For attributed outcomes and credited revenue use `/api/v1/breakdown` or `/api/v1/overview`.

`filter[<dimension>]=<operator>:<value>` narrows the window to the same slice the dashboard would show. The range is inclusive of `date_to`, like every other route here.

get.summary: Get the messaging-cohort (DM Ads) KPI rollup
get.description:
The headline numbers for messaging-objective ads: spend, conversations started, how many were intent-scored, how many scored high-intent, and the resulting cost per high-intent conversation.

Sits beside `GET /api/v1/attribution/messaging`, which lists the individual messaging-attributed conversions, and reads a DIFFERENT source: the messaging cohort of the creative feature store rather than the modeled-credit ledger.

**It can answer 200 with `available: false`,** and that is not an error. The source is a ROLLING aggregate over 7/14/28-day or lifetime buckets ending at the last rebuild, so a range ending more than two days in the past gets `stale_window` rather than numbers that silently describe a different period. A profile with no messaging cohort gets `no_messaging_data`. Every metric is null in both cases — null, not 0, because neither is a measurement.

**There is no previous-period comparison parameter.** The rolling source has no date-bound breakdown to compute a delta from, so rather than accept and ignore `prev_from`/`prev_to`, this route does not offer them.

`spend` is denominated in the profile's reporting currency and is returned as a number: this API does not format money.

get.description:
How this profile's traffic is labelled into channels, and the vocabulary those labels come from.

Rules are returned in EVALUATION order — `priority` ascending, first match wins — so a client can render the ladder without re-sorting.

The taxonomy ships in the same response because a rule cannot be read without it: `output_channel` is always one of its `channel_name` values, and a separate route would let a client draw a rule whose channel it cannot name.

**Two matchers coexist.** `conditions` is the structured form the current editor writes; the flat `source_pattern` / `medium_pattern` / … columns are the older form that live rows still carry. Render whichever the row has — collapsing them makes old rules look empty.

No date range: rules are configuration, not a window.

**`output_channel` must already be in the taxonomy** — `GET /api/v1/channel-rules` returns it, and `POST /api/v1/channel-taxonomy` adds to it. A rule pointing at a channel that does not exist would classify traffic into a label nothing can render.

**Preview before you save.** `POST /api/v1/channel-rules/match-count` says how much traffic one condition set catches, and `POST /api/v1/channel-rules/diff` says what a whole candidate ladder would re-label. Pass the diff's counts back as `diff_summary` and they are recorded on the audit row.

get.summary: Get instrumentation health
get.description:
Whether the measurement itself can be trusted: is the site tracker firing, is identity stitching, are click IDs arriving, does checkout metadata reach the payment provider, and is every cash conversion FX-normalized. Six signals, a 0-100 rolled-up `score`, a `verdict`, and `missing` — the machine-readable list of what is dead or incomplete.

READ IT BEFORE ACTING ON ANY COVERAGE OR ROAS NUMBER. A low traceable-cash percentage means "you have great organic" when `tracking_healthy` is true and "your tracking is broken" when it is false, and the two call for opposite responses. `coverage_interpretation` states which in one field.

THE SAME DOCUMENT `GET /api/v1/trust` RETURNS AS ITS `instrumentation` LEG, byte for byte — one RPC, one transform. Use `/trust` when you want the coverage number and this caveat together over one date range; use this one when the WINDOW is the question, e.g. re-checking after a fix, where `/trust` would make you invent a date range and pay for two reads you do not render.

`?days=` is capped to the Ephemeral Buffer's retention (30 days, ADR 0014 d2) because one of the six signals counts rows in `events_enriched`, which is pruned at 30 days. A wider request is REJECTED (400) rather than silently narrowed — the RPC would answer over 30 days either way, and a silently narrowed window is a number that lies about what it measured.

get.description:
The review queue: pairs of customer profiles a scan believes are the same person, newest first, each with both sides' identity and the evidence for the match.

**Keyset paginated.** Pass the `cursor` from `pagination.cursor` to walk older pages; an unreadable cursor starts from the beginning rather than erroring. There is no total — the queue is being resolved while you walk it, so an offset page would shift under you.

`status_counts` rides alongside `data` and describes the WHOLE queue, ignoring `?status=` on purpose: it is what renders "Pending (12) / Snoozed (3)" while one tab is open.

Scope: `customers:read`. A proposal names two people with their emails and phones, and there is no useful masked variant — remove the identity and a merge review has nothing left to review.

Re-scans this profile's customers for pairs that look like the same person and refills the review queue.

A WRITE — it inserts new proposals, supersedes older ones a better match replaced, and resurfaces snoozed ones whose window expired — but it merges nothing and moves no attribution credit, so it enqueues no recompute. The three counts are disjoint; a run that finds nothing new is three zeros, not an error.

No body: the scan is over the credential's own profile, and there is nothing else to name.

Scopes: `customers:read` AND `attribution:write` — the same pair every write on this surface carries.

get.description:
Counts, computed NOW, of what merging this proposal's two customers would move: outcome events, identifiers, touches, conversions and cash revenue, plus the three things that are lossy — a lead that would coalesce, and an email or phone collision the survivor's value wins.

Deliberately not the same numbers as the proposal's `evidence`: that is what was true when the proposal was raised, this is what is true today.

Read-only. Deciding is `POST …/decide`.

post.summary: Merge, dismiss or snooze a suggested merge
post.description:
`merge` performs the merge and resolves the proposal; `dismiss` resolves it without merging; `snooze` hides it for 30 days and lets the next scan resurface it.

`survivor_profile_id` overrides which of the two customers survives — pass the other side's id when the proposal picked the wrong one. It must be one of the two; anything else is 422.

**A merge is not reversible from this endpoint.** It moves the merged customer's outcome events, identifiers, touches and conversions onto the survivor and enqueues an attribution recompute, because moving those rows moves attribution credit. `GET /api/v1/identity/merge-history` records what happened.

**Idempotent.** A proposal that is no longer `pending` was already decided: the call writes nothing and answers 200 with `changed: false` and the status it already holds. A retry after a dropped response must not read as an error, which is also why re-merging an already-merged pair is not a 409.

Scopes: `customers:read` AND `attribution:write`. The first because the proposal is about two named people; the second because the merge moves attribution credit — the same scope `POST /api/v1/exports` and the first-payment override carry.

get.description:
Scores every non-merged customer profile: how many are missing a primary email or phone, how many duplicate-email/phone groups exist, and — per profile — what a backfill would write.

`auto_repairable_count` counts BACKFILLS only. Merges left the bulk repair path and go through the proposal queue instead, so `auto_merge_count` is reported for awareness and is not something `POST /api/v1/identity/repair` will act on.

Offset paginated (`page`/`page_size`), because the underlying scan is a single ranked snapshot rather than a stream — unlike the proposal queue, walking it twice sees the same population.

Scope: `customers:read` — every row names a person.

post.summary: Preview or apply identity repairs
post.description:
`action: "preview"` computes what would change and writes nothing; `action: "apply"` performs it. The two take the same body so a caller can preview exactly what it is about to apply.

**Omit `operations` for the AUTO set** — every safe primary-email/primary-phone backfill the scan found. Merges are excluded from that set by design: a merge is a per-pair review decision, not a bulk repair.

**Pass `operations` to name them yourself**, including `merge_profiles` — this is the path a manual merge of two specific customers takes.

**A skipped operation is not an error.** An operation whose precondition moved since the preview (the value is already set, the pair is already merged) lands in `skipped` with the reason while the rest apply, which is what makes the call safe to retry.

An apply that merged anything enqueues an attribution recompute; a backfill-only apply does not, because it moves no credit.

Scopes: `customers:read` AND `attribution:write` — for BOTH actions. A preview is read-only but is a step in a write flow, and the response names the same people the apply will move.

get.summary: Poll a hand-off you handed to a human
get.description:
Some steps only a human can take — granting an OAuth consent, picking a Meta ad account, signing a DPA, paying for a plan, approving a write you proposed. Each of those is minted as a **hand-off**: you get a URL, give it to your user, and poll here until they are done.

**There is no `POST /api/v1/handoffs`.** A hand-off is created by the route for the thing it hands off, which is the only place that knows what completing it means. This is the one poll they all share.

**An expired hand-off is 200 with `status: "expired"`, never 404.** Expiry is derived at read time, so there is no window in which a dead hand-off still reads `pending`, and no ambiguity between 'this one lapsed, mint another' and 'that id is wrong'.

**`url` is returned only while `status` is `pending`.** Whoever holds it can complete the hand-off — the page is session-less by design, so your user does not need an Atribu account or an open session — which is exactly why a settled hand-off stops returning it.

A hand-off minted by another workspace is 404, the same answer an id that never existed gets.

Scope: `connections:read` OR `analytics:read`. The mint is what needs authority, not the question about it — but the `connect` kind (#1046) is minted under `connections:write`, so this poll accepts `connections:read` alongside `analytics:read` for the same reason the rest of the connect rail dual-accepts: a credential minted with only the `connections` core scope must be able to read back a hand-off it just started.

schema.description: The `handoff_id` the minting call returned. Not the handle the URL carries — that is the human's capability, this is the agent's.

parameters.description: The `handoff_id` the minting call returned. Not the handle the URL carries — that is the human's capability, this is the agent's.
parameters.name: id

200.description: The hand-off, in whatever state it is in

404.description: No hand-off with that id for this workspace — never created, malformed, or minted by someone else. The three are deliberately indistinguishable. An EXPIRED hand-off is not one of them: that is a 200.

post.summary: Hand a provider connect to a human and get a URL for them
post.description:
Your agent cannot grant an OAuth consent — the provider's screen needs a person in a browser. This mints a **hand-off**: give the returned `url` to your user, then poll `GET /api/v1/handoffs/{id}` until `status` is no longer `pending`.

**The page is session-less.** Whoever holds the link completes it — signed out, on a phone, without an Atribu account. That is the point: the human you are handing this to is often the client, not the operator.

**Two ways it completes, and both answer `status: "completed"`.** When the consent resolves to exactly one account, `result.connection_id` names the connection that was written — read it with `GET /api/v1/connections/{id}`. When it exposes several, `result.pending_selection` says so and a human choice is still owed: finish it with `GET /api/v1/connections/pending/{provider}` and `POST …/finalize` (the parked provider token lives 60 minutes). The hand-off is `completed` either way, because the part only a browser could do is done.

**Every ending comes back to your app (#1800).** Send your user to `start_url` (not `url`) with a `return_url`, and they meet the provider's consent screen and then your `return_url` — never a page of ours. The bounce carries `?connect=<slug>&provider=<provider>&status=<status>&profile_id=<id>&handoff_id=<id>`, plus `reason` on `failed`/`cancelled` and `candidate_count` on `pending_selection`. `status` is `success`, `pending_selection`, `failed`, or `cancelled` (the user cancelled on the provider's screen).

**`reason` is one list, on the bounce and on your poll's `result.reason` alike:** `user_cancelled`, `provider_denied`, `provider_error`, `token_exchange_failed`, `account_connected_elsewhere`, `no_candidates`, `connect_failed`, `internal_error`, `state_expired`, `state_invalid`, `handoff_expired`, `handoff_used`, `provider_not_configured`, `origin_not_allowed`. A cancel settles the hand-off `cancelled`; every other reason settles it `failed`. `origin_not_allowed` is poll-only — there is no registered target to bounce to, which is the refusal.

**The URL is single-use and short-lived.** It stops working at `expires_at` (45 minutes) and the moment the hand-off settles — success, failure or cancel. One consent per hand-off: if your user finishes two (a double-click), exactly one is used and the other normally reports its outcome; the bounce is a hint, so confirm with the poll. A consent that stops partway on our side frees the link again after 3 minutes. A second click on a COMPLETED hand-off normally bounces its real outcome; one that ended `failed`/`cancelled` bounces `handoff_used`, an expired one `handoff_expired`. `internal_error` is transient and does not settle the hand-off — retry the same link. Mint another to retry anything else — minting twice is two hand-offs, not an error.

Scope: `attribution:write` — the same scope the connect picker declares, so one credential can start a connect and finish it.

schema.description: The `connection_provider` value — the same string `GET /api/v1/connections` returns as `channel`, so a connection you read back can be fed straight into a re-connect. `shopify` (#2104) needs `shop` in the body: Shopify's consent lives on the merchant's own store, so Atribu cannot start it without knowing which one.

parameters.description: The `connection_provider` value — the same string `GET /api/v1/connections` returns as `channel`, so a connection you read back can be fed straight into a re-connect. `shopify` (#2104) needs `shop` in the body: Shopify's consent lives on the merchant's own store, so Atribu cannot start it without knowing which one.
parameters.name: provider

profile_id.description: Optional assertion, not a selector. Your credential already names a profile; sending a DIFFERENT one is 404. Omit it unless you want the request to fail loudly when your key is scoped somewhere you did not expect.

return_url.description: Where to send the human when the consent ends — success, failure or cancel — instead of back to the hand-off page. Must be an absolute http(s) URL whose ORIGIN your app can receive the bounce on for this profile: any origin from your app's own `redirect_uris` works automatically, and `allowed_return_origins` narrows that set or adds an origin your `redirect_uris` don't cover. Checked HERE (#1800): an origin outside both sets, a profile no app governs, or — for a delegated key — a profile governed by a different app than the key's is a 400. It is re-checked when the human clicks, and only a registration changed in between can still end the hand-off `failed` with `result.reason: "origin_not_allowed"`.

shop.description: `shopify` only, and REQUIRED there (#2104): the store to install on — its `<handle>.myshopify.com` domain, the bare handle, or a pasted admin URL. A custom storefront domain is a 400: Shopify's install runs on the myshopify domain. The merchant consents to Atribu's Shopify app — or, when Atribu has registered a custom-distribution app for that store, to that one — and lands back on your `return_url` with no Atribu login and no plan page. The store's lifecycle then reaches your `atribu` subscription as `connection.connected` / `connection.revoked` (uninstall) / `connection.reconnect_required`, with `data.provider: "shopify"`. Ignored for every other provider.

200.description: The hand-off. `start_url` is where a partner app sends its user (straight to the provider's consent); `url` is the page you give a human directly; `id` is what you poll. Identical to what `GET /api/v1/handoffs/{id}` returns.

400.description: `provider` is not one of the seven, `shop` is missing or not a store handle for `shopify`, or `return_url` is not an absolute http(s) URL on an origin registered for this profile's app (and, for a delegated key, the key's own app).

404.description: `profile_id` names a profile this credential is not scoped to. The same answer a profile that does not exist gets — deliberately indistinguishable.

422.description: The request body is present but is not a JSON object.

get.summary: Read a CRM's pipeline stages with the suggested and current outcome mapping
get.description:
Everything a «map your CRM stages» screen needs, in one read: every stage of every pipeline of every connected location, what Atribu suggests each stage means (with a label ready to show), the mapping in force, and — when there is no suggestion — why not.

**Writing the mapping** is `PATCH /api/v1/outcome-definitions/{outcome_definition_id}` with `{"event_key": "<outcomes[].key>"}`, one row per stage. It is idempotent: the same body twice leaves the same row, so applying every suggestion is safe to retry. The write needs `goals:write` and the attribution entitlement; `can_write` and each stage's `writable` say up front whether it would be refused.

Reads Atribu's own copy of the pipelines (refreshed on every CRM sync), never the CRM live, and calls no model: it is cheap and the same stage name always gets the same suggestion.

**Before auto-applying**, skip stages whose `current.source` is `user` (someone chose them) and treat `engine_default` as unset.

`provider`: `gohighlevel`. Any other value is 404.

Scope: `connections:read` or `analytics:read`.

post.summary: Mint a signing hand-off for the Data Processing Agreement
post.description:
Your agent cannot agree to a contract on a customer's behalf, so it mints a **hand-off**: a session-less URL for a person, an id to poll, and an expiry. The page renders the same click-wrap the console shows — scroll to the bottom, give a name and an email, accept — and records the signer's email, IP, user agent, timestamp and document version.

**A document that is already accepted answers `status: "completed"` immediately**, with `result: { already_accepted: true }` and no URL. That is the idempotent path: re-running a checklist must never ask a customer to sign twice.

Poll `GET /api/v1/handoffs/{id}` until `status` leaves `pending`, then read the record back from `GET /api/v1/conversion-sync/legal`.

Scope: `exports:write` — the legal half of the Conversion Sync surface, whose read is `exports:read`.

200.description: The hand-off. `status: "pending"` with a `url` to hand over, or `status: "completed"` with `result.already_accepted` when it was signed already.

post.summary: Accept the Data Processing Agreement as the signed-in owner or admin
post.description:
Records a click-wrap acceptance **for the signed-in person making the call**. This is the console's own write, exposed so acceptance has one implementation rather than several.

**An API key or an MCP token is refused with 403.** A machine credential — a delegated key most of all, which is an app acting for someone else's workspace — is not a person who can agree to a contract, and a signature record that could have been produced by one would be worth nothing. An `atb_user_` MCP token is refused too, and deliberately: it names a real person but it is the credential they minted FOR AN AGENT, so accepting with one is an agent signing on their behalf. Only a browser session says a person is present. Mint a hand-off with `POST /api/v1/legal/{document}/handoff` and give the URL to a human instead.

Session callers must hold the workspace role `owner` or `admin`; a guest reaching the profile through a profile membership alone is refused for the same reason.

**Idempotent**: accepting an already-accepted document writes nothing and answers `already_accepted: true` with the ORIGINAL timestamp.

The body is optional. Its one field, `document_version`, names WHICH of the shipped texts you displayed — the full agreement at `/dpa`, or the shorter platform-safe click-wrap that gates `privacy_mode`. It is checked against an allowlist and never recorded as given: the column says which agreement a customer accepted, and it cannot do that if the customer picks the value. Omit it to accept the current text.

403.description: The credential is an API key (a machine cannot sign), the caller is not a workspace owner/admin, or the exports:write scope is missing

422.description: document_version is not a version of this document that this build ships

post.summary: Mint a Stripe Checkout hand-off for a plan upgrade
post.description:
Your agent cannot enter a card, so it mints a **hand-off**: a Stripe Checkout URL to give a person, an id to poll, and an expiry. The human pays in any browser, Stripe's webhook settles the hand-off, and your next poll answers `status: "completed"` with `result.subscription` naming the new tier and status.

**Already on that plan?** The hand-off comes back `completed` with `result: { no_change: true }` and no URL — never a second subscription. `trialing` counts as being on the plan: a mid-trial workspace already holds that subscription, and buying it again would create a second one rather than converting the trial.

**API keys cannot call this.** The route is workspace-scoped and a key is minted for one profile, so it has no workspace membership to check — `withApiAuth` refuses it with a 403 before the handler runs. A signed-in session and an MCP user token (`atb_user_`) both reach it: each names a PERSON with a workspace role, and the MCP `start_plan_upgrade` tool rides the same route. The caller must hold the workspace role `owner` or `admin`: an analyst reads numbers and does not commit the workspace to a recurring charge.

**Downgrades are not a checkout.** A lower tier is a Customer Portal change; opening a second subscription for it would double-bill. `upgrade_available` on the subscription read lists only what is above the current plan for exactly this reason.

The Checkout URL is never returned after the hand-off settles — a spent Stripe session renders an error page, and handing one back would advertise a dead payment link.

Scope: `analytics:read`, matching the subscription read this answers. The scope is not the gate here; the workspace role is.

200.description: The hand-off. `status: "pending"` with the Checkout `url` to hand over, or `status: "completed"` with `result.no_change` when the plan is already active.

403.description: The credential is an API key (single-profile by design), or the caller is not a workspace owner/admin

404.description: The workspace does not exist, or you are not an active member

422.description: Unknown plan or interval

post.summary: Open Stripe's Customer Portal for a workspace
post.description:
Returns a single-use, short-lived URL to Stripe's hosted billing console, where the payer can change their card, switch or cancel the plan, and download invoices.

**Not a hand-off, unlike the checkout above, and the asymmetry is deliberate.** A checkout is an act an agent can PREPARE and a human completes later, which is what makes a pending action the right shape. The portal is a management console for someone already signed in and already looking at their billing page: there is nothing to poll and nothing to settle, and a portal URL handed to a third party is an account-management link to a subscription they do not own. Give this URL to the person who asked for it, or to nobody.

**A downgrade lives here, not in the checkout.** Opening a second subscription for a lower tier would double-bill, which is why the subscription read's `upgrade_available` lists only what is above the current plan.

**API keys cannot call this**, and the caller must be a workspace `owner` or `admin` — both for the reasons the checkout route above states. The portal is where a subscription is cancelled; it is not a lighter act than starting one.

PREREQUISITE: the Customer Portal must be configured in the Stripe Dashboard (Settings → Billing → Customer Portal) for this mode. Without it Stripe refuses, and the 502 carries Stripe's own sentence naming what to create.

403.description: The credential is an API key, the caller is not a workspace owner/admin, or the workspace bills through Shopify

404.description: The workspace does not exist, or you are not an active member

409.description: The workspace has no Stripe customer, so there is no portal to open. Start a subscription first.

502.description: Stripe refused the request — most often an unconfigured Customer Portal

503.description: Billing is not configured on this deployment; no session was created

get.summary: List a profile's manual Shopify webhook connections
get.description:
Manual mode (#412) is for merchants who will not install a third-party app — agency-managed client stores, Plus orgs with an app-approval policy. Shopify's admin lets them create webhooks by hand with no app involved, signed with a **per-store signing ID** rather than the app's client secret.

Returns one entry per manual connection on the profile, with the URL to paste, the topics to create, and the delivery state. App Store installs are not manual connections and never appear here.

Scope: `analytics:read`, matching the connection reads beside it.

post.summary: Create a manual Shopify webhook connection
post.description:
Mints the inbound token and returns the URL the merchant pastes into Shopify. The connection is usable the moment its signing ID is set (PATCH below) — until then deliveries arrive and are rejected, which is what `state: "pending"` reports.

**Idempotent on the shop domain.** Repeating the same `shop_domain` returns the existing connection with `200` rather than minting a second token; only a genuinely new connection answers `201`. A shop already connected through the App Store install answers `409`: a manual twin would give the store two verification paths, one of them with no signing ID.

Seeding the profile's default `conversion_definitions` rides along, for the reason the App Store install does it (#437): a profile with none captures orders perfectly and produces zero conversions.

Scope: `attribution:write`, matching the connection writes beside it.

200.description: An identical manual connection already existed; it is returned unchanged

409.description: The shop is already connected through the Shopify App Store install

422.description: `shop_domain` is not a legal Shopify store handle

patch.summary: Store the store's webhook signing ID
patch.description:
The signing ID is printed at the bottom of Shopify admin → Settings → Notifications → Webhooks, and it is what every delivery's `X-Shopify-Hmac-SHA256` is computed with. **Write-only**: no route returns it, and the list read reports only `signing_id_configured`.

Setting a new one clears `last_hmac_failure_at` — the previous failures are stale history the moment the merchant fixes the cause, and leaving them up would keep warning about a problem that is solved.

Scope: `attribution:write`.

404.description: No such manual connection on this profile

delete.summary: Remove a manual Shopify webhook connection
delete.description:
**Disconnects, it does not delete.** The row is what historical `outcome_events` were ingested against, and removing it would orphan that attribution — the same rule the app uninstall follows. Clearing the metadata also retires the inbound token, so a webhook the merchant forgets to delete in Shopify stops resolving.

Scope: `attribution:write`.

404.description: No such manual connection on this profile

post.summary: Re-run the Shopify app pixel installation
post.description:
Calls `webPixelCreate` (or `webPixelUpdate`) on the connected store with the profile's active tracking key. Use it when the merchant sees the App Pixel as **Disconnected** in Shopify's Settings → Customer events even though the store is connected: a race during install, no tracking key at the time, or a pixel the merchant deleted.

Per Shopify's docs an app pixel is auto-registered at install and stays "Disconnected" until `webPixelCreate` is called. There is no snippet to paste and no custom-pixel step — that is a different, legacy pixel type.

`success: false` with an `error` is a normal outcome, not a transport failure: Shopify returns `userErrors` for a store the app cannot pixel (no released extension, for instance), and the message is Shopify's own.

Scope: `tracking:write` — configuring a site's tracking installation is exactly what that scope names.

422.description: No active Shopify connection on the profile, no stored credentials, or no active tracking key

502.description: Shopify's Admin API refused the request; the message is Shopify's own

post.summary: Choose a plan on a Shopify App Store workspace
post.description:
The Shopify counterpart to `POST /api/v1/workspaces/{workspaceId}/checkout-session`, and the two are mutually exclusive: a workspace bills through exactly one rail, chosen by how it was acquired. This route **refuses** any workspace that did not arrive through the App Store install (403), and the checkout route refuses one that did.

**Paid tiers are sold by Shopify, not by us.** Once an app opts in to Managed Pricing, `appSubscriptionCreate` is rejected outright, so the only correct answer for `growth` or `agency` is an absolute link to Shopify's hosted plan page — the merchant confirms the actual tier there and the `app_subscriptions/update` webhook mirrors the result. Which paid tier you name therefore does not decide anything.

**`free` is different.** It is not a Shopify-billed tier: it writes a $0 subscription on the internal starter limits, touches the Billing API not at all, and answers with a relative PATH into the app. A workspace with a live Shopify subscription answers `409` instead — that charge must be cancelled from the Shopify admin first.

**API keys cannot call this**, for the reason the checkout route states: it is workspace-scoped and a key is minted for one profile. The caller must be a workspace `owner` or `admin`.

200.description: Where to send the merchant — an absolute Shopify admin URL for a paid tier, a relative app path for `free`

403.description: The credential is an API key, the caller is not a workspace owner/admin, or the workspace does not bill through the Shopify App Store

404.description: The workspace does not exist, is archived, or you are not a member

409.description: A live Shopify subscription blocks the switch to `free`

422.description: Unknown plan, or no Shopify connection on the workspace

get.summary: List tracked competitor handles and hashtags
get.description:
Every competitor source on this profile, enabled and disabled, newest first (max 200).

`media_count` rides along so a list render needs no second call per row. Read its field note before treating `null` as zero.

post.summary: Track a competitor handle or hashtag
post.description:
`value` is normalised before it is stored — lowercased, with a leading `@` or `#` removed — so two spellings of the same handle collide on the unique constraint rather than becoming near-duplicates.

**The charset is enforced, and that is not cosmetic.** Characters outside Meta's username/hashtag policy flow into the Graph `fields` expression unencoded; Meta answers 400, the nightly sync swallows that as "0 rows synced" and CLEARS `last_sync_error` — so a malformed source looks healthy forever.

Capped per profile (50 by default): Business Discovery and Hashtag Search are APP-level rate limited, so one tenant with hundreds of handles starves every other tenant's nightly sync.

Scope: `instagram`.

409.description: Already tracked, or the per-profile cap is reached

patch.summary: Enable, disable or relabel a competitor source
patch.description:
Supply at least one of `enabled` or `display_label`. A source belonging to another profile is 404, indistinguishable from one that does not exist.

`media_count` is `null` on this response — it is not recomputed for a metadata edit, and a stale number would be worse than no number.

Scope: `instagram`.

delete.description:
Deletes the source. Captured `ig_competitor_media` snapshots are removed with it by the FK cascade.

**404 on an id this profile does not own**, unlike the internal handler this replaces, which answered `{ ok: true }` either way and so made a typo'd id indistinguishable from a successful removal.

Scope: `instagram`.

404.description: No such row on this profile

get.summary: Latest captured posts for one competitor source
get.description:
The most recent snapshot day only, up to 25 posts, most-liked first. An empty array means this source has never returned a post — there is no snapshot day to read.

Scope: `instagram`.

post.summary: Queue a competitor-research sync now
post.description:
Enqueues ONE `competitor_research` job for this profile's Instagram connection — the same message the nightly tick sends. Enqueue-only: the pipeline-worker is woken by LISTEN/NOTIFY, so nothing here waits on Meta.

Two guards, and both answer rather than silently no-op: a job already pending for the connection returns `already_queued`, and a refresh inside the 60-second per-connection cooldown is a 429 carrying `Retry-After` in seconds.

Scope: `instagram`.

get.summary: List Instagram short links
get.description:
The profile's `/r/<slug>` links, newest first (max 200). `base_url` is the origin the slugs resolve against — the main app's, never the API's — so a caller can build the full URL without hardcoding a host.

Scope: `instagram`.

post.summary: Mint an Instagram short link
post.description:
`destination_url` passes a scheme + host ALLOWLIST, not just a URL shape: http(s) only, and no loopback, private, link-local or cloud-metadata host. This value is later redirected to and embedded in a public page, and a plain URL check accepts `javascript:`, `data:` and `169.254.169.254`.

**Idempotent per media.** With `ig_media_id`, a second call returns the existing reservation (patched to the destination and UTMs you sent) with `reused: true` and **200**, not 201. Pinning a `slug` that disagrees with that reservation is a 409 instead — merge-on-conflict is the semantic for an unspecified slug only.

Scope: `instagram`.

200.description: An existing per-media reservation was returned (`reused: true`)

400.description: `destination_url` is not an allowed public http(s) URL

409.description: The requested slug is taken, or conflicts with the media's reservation

post.summary: Mint a Follow Proxy link for an Instagram handle
post.description:
A short link whose destination is `instagram.com/<handle>`, for the Website URL field of a Meta Website-Traffic ad. The click carries UTMs and stamps the visitor cookie on the redirect, which is what later joins a Follow→DM event to the ad that paid for it.

Idempotent per (profile, handle): re-issuing returns the existing slug with `reused: true` and 200 rather than minting a second one.

Scope: `instagram`.

ig_username.description: With or without a leading `@`; normalised to lowercase.

200.description: The existing Follow Proxy link (`reused: true`)

400.description: `ig_username` is not a valid Instagram handle

patch.summary: Show or hide one post on the hosted bio page
patch.description:
Toggles `ig_media.visible_on_bio` for one synced post, which is what the hosted `/bio/<slug>` page renders from.

`media_id` is the META media id (a numeric string), not an Atribu uuid. The path is `/bio-media/` rather than a longer path under `/instagram/media/` on purpose: that prefix is the live Graph proxy, and a rewrite capturing a longer path under it would be one ordering mistake away from forwarding that route here.

Scope: `instagram`.

get.summary: List connected Instagram accounts
get.description:
Every Instagram binding on this profile, newest first, each carrying the health of the `data_connections` row behind it so a settings render needs no second call.

delete.description:
Deletes the binding (cascading to the conversations tied to it) and marks the `data_connections` row `disconnected` rather than deleting it — the row stays as the audit record, which is the convention every provider's disconnect follows.

If this binding owned the account's automations and the same Instagram account is still connected from another workspace, the oldest surviving healthy binding is promoted, so comment-to-DM and the AI agent resume there instead of going dark.

Scope: `instagram`.

`next_cursor` is the last row's `posted_at`; pass it as `?after=`. `connection_status` and `last_synced_at` ride along because the post picker polls this endpoint while a sync runs — a separate call for them would be a poll per poll.

**Both halves are cleared.** The send path short-circuits on a Redis key BEFORE it looks at `comment_to_dm_paused_until`, so clearing only the column would answer 200 and leave the account paused.

A trigger fires when a comment on this account matches `keyword` under `keyword_match_mode`, sending `opening_message` as a DM (and optionally `public_comment_reply` on the comment itself).

`post_id_allowlist` restricts it to named posts; omit it and every post is in scope. Sends are capped per account per minute by the circuit breaker — see the resume route.

post.description:
Sends the trigger's `opening_message` to one Instagram user (by IGSID) with Meta's HUMAN_AGENT tag, without counting as a trigger fire. Meta only accepts it when that person messaged the account in the last 7 days; otherwise the send is refused and the Meta error is returned.

get.summary: Click-to-Message attribution health
get.description:
How many of this profile's Instagram conversations were attributed DETERMINISTICALLY — an exact DM-ad referral or a Follow Proxy click — against every conversation in the window, plus the counts each other attribution path contributed.

`severity` is `empty` when there is nothing to measure, `critical` when a webhook delivery has failed recently (whatever the ratio), otherwise `ok` at ≥60% deterministic, `warn` at ≥30%, `critical` below. **`empty` is not a bad score**; it means the window holds no Instagram conversations at all.

Every MESSAGES-objective Meta ad on this profile, flagged with whether ManyChat holds a flow mapping for it. An unmapped ad is one whose conversations cannot be attributed deterministically, which is what makes this list actionable rather than descriptive.

Scope: `instagram`.

200.description: The inventory and its mapped/unmapped split

get.summary: Which ads produced followers
get.description:
Expected followers per ad with a confidence band, plus the window's total follow events.

**Read `coverage_note` before quoting these numbers.** Follow events are captured through a welcome-DM heuristic, so only followers who DM the business are scored — Meta does not expose the `follow` webhook field to Instagram Business Login apps, and silent followers are absent from this attribution entirely. The caveat is served with the data rather than left to a UI to remember.

Scope: `instagram`.

get.description:
The queue of proposed matches between an Instagram DM sender and a customer profile, each carrying the evidence (username, and the email or phone extracted from the thread).

post.description:
Approving STITCHES the DM's identity onto the customer profile — it merges identities and is what unlocks modeled attribution from a DM conversation to a payment. Rejecting closes the review and leaves both identities alone.

The review's ownership is re-checked against your profile before the merge runs: the underlying routine keys only on the review id, so the scope gate alone would not be enough.

post.summary: Queue an Instagram sync now
post.description:
Enqueues this profile's Instagram sync jobs — the same messages the daily tick sends. **202, because the work is accepted, not done**: the pipeline-worker is woken by LISTEN/NOTIFY and nothing here waits on Meta. Poll `GET /api/v1/instagram/accounts/{account_id}/media` for `connection_status` and `last_synced_at` to see it finish.

Zero jobs enqueued is a 409, not a 202 with a count of nothing: it means a sync is already running for the connection.

get.summary: Per-key API usage for a workspace
get.description:
What each of this workspace's API keys did over a date range: request count, the 4xx/5xx split, p50/p95 latency and when it was last seen.

**Workspace-scoped, so a session bearer or an MCP user token only.** An API key names exactly one profile and has no workspace to read across; it receives 403 `insufficient_scope`.

Counts are within one flush window of live (the writer batches, at most 5 seconds or 200 requests behind). The 4xx/5xx SHARE is unaffected by that lag — a delayed batch delays successes and errors alike.

Rows older than 90 days are pruned, so a window reaching further back returns only what is still retained.

get.summary: List the profile's click-to-WhatsApp ads
get.description:
Every click-to-WhatsApp ad on this profile: which ones open WhatsApp, the number and Page they open, the call-to-action they carry, and the greeting ("Saludo automático") each shows the customer BEFORE they type anything.

An ad is listed when WhatsApp is named either by its ad set's `destination_type` or by its creative's call-to-action — the two are set in different places by different people and an ad commonly carries only one of them.

SCOPING: the credential is the tenant selection, exactly as on `GET /api/v1/partner/whatsapp/ads/{ad_id}/welcome-message` and `POST /api/v1/partner/wa-joins`. There is no `profile_id` parameter — every Atribu key is profile-scoped, so a multi-tenant consumer sends the per-connection token carrying the right profile rather than one global key.

This is served from what Atribu's nightly structure sync already read, so refreshing a screen costs the advertiser's `ads_management` quota nothing. `last_synced_at` on each row says how stale that is; an ad launched since the last sync is not listed yet, and its greeting is still readable by id on the welcome-message route.

post.summary: Apply Atribu's URL parameters to Meta ads
post.description:
Writes Atribu's URL parameters onto up to 25 Meta ads, MERGED with each ad's own: every parameter the ad already has that Atribu does not own is kept verbatim, and Atribu's keys (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, utm_content, utm_id) take Atribu's `{{…}}` id macros.

**What Meta does with the edit.** URL parameters live on the ad's creative, and Meta does not let an existing creative's `url_tags` be edited. Atribu therefore creates a new creative from the ad's SAME page post (so its likes, comments and shares stay) with the merged parameters and points the ad at it. Meta counts a creative change as a significant edit: it can restart the ad set's learning phase, and the ad goes through Meta's review again. So every call must carry `acknowledge_learning_reset: true`.

Each ad carries `expected_url_tags` — the current value shown to the person. Meta's live value is read first; when it differs the ad is `skipped` (`changed_since_preview`) and nothing is written. Re-applying is safe: an ad that already carries the parameters is `skipped` (`already_applied`).

One result per ad, in request order. A Meta refusal is that ad's `failed` result, not an HTTP error. Undo one ad with `POST /api/v1/quality/ad-ids/url-tags/undo`.

expected_url_tags.description: The ad's CURRENT URL parameters as shown to the person (`missing_macro[].url_tags`); null when it has none.

reason.description: Why a `skipped` ad was not changed. `already_applied`: it already carries Atribu's parameters (a re-apply is a no-op). `changed_since_preview`: its live parameters differ from `expected_url_tags` — show `suggested_url_tags` and ask again. `dynamic_creative` / `catalog_ad` / `no_post`: the creative cannot be rebuilt from its post — copy the parameters in Ads Manager. `write_permission_missing`: the Meta connection is read-only. `no_connection`, `not_found`, `no_creative`: nothing to write through or to.

get.summary: Replay outcome.recorded events
get.description:
The `outcome.recorded` events of this profile — every GoHighLevel and MercadoPago outcome Atribu recorded for it since the event existed — in ledger (recording) order — the order the webhook enqueues them; retries can deliver pushes out of order — from an opaque cursor. Use it to backfill a new subscriber, or to reconcile after downtime: the ids are the webhook's, so de-duping on `id` makes the two paths safe to mix.

**Resuming.** `pagination.cursor` is returned on every page that has a position, including the last. Store it and pass it back later; `has_next: false` means you are caught up, not that the feed ended. Omit `cursor` to start from the first event. A cursor this endpoint did not issue is `400 invalid_parameter` (never a silent restart).

**Order.** Events appear once their transaction is settled, in recording order, and never behind a cursor you already hold.

**The scope decides the shape.** `conversions:read` opens the read with the person left out (`contact: null`, `contact_withheld: true`, and a `customer_key` that is not the provider's opaque id set to `null`); `customers:read` adds the person.

**Healthcare.** A healthcare-family profile (a healthcare workspace, or a profile in Platform-Safe / HIPAA privacy mode) is served only to a key of the app that provisioned it; any other caller, whatever its scopes, gets `403 healthcare_scope_forbidden`. That app's key never carries `customers:read` there, so the person is added when the app's grant on the profile opens contact (the webhook's rule), and that read is recorded in the PII access log. When the profile's privacy settings, the app that provisioned it or its grant cannot be read the answer is `503`, never a page without the check.

Only profiles provisioned by an app produce events, and only outcomes recorded after this endpoint shipped. Each event stays replayable for 90 days after it was delivered; an erased customer's events are not replayed.
